ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA) is red‑cell destruction in small vessels, producing schistocytes, low platelets and often organ injury. It is a clinical emergency that requires rapid cause‑specific treatment.

sections.p: MAHA is haemolysis caused by mechanical damage to red cells as they pass through narrowed or fibrin‑laden microvasculature. Diagnosis is clinical plus a peripheral smear showing schistocytes and evidence of haemolysis (high LDH, low haptoglobin).

Severity is gauged by organ involvement and haemolysis extent. The classic pentad (thrombocytopenia, MAHA, renal failure, fever, neuro deficits) signals severe disease. Early stages may have only haemolysis and thrombocytopenia.
b: Moderate: add renal dysfunction or fever

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, the top causes are infections (malaria, HIV, TB), rheumatic heart disease, and herbal toxins. Systemic conditions like TTP, HUS, DIC, and severe hypertension also rank high.

t.b: Negative in MAHA, positive in autoimmune haemolysis

sections.p: Patients often appear jaundiced, pale, with bruising. They may have fever, flank pain, altered mental status, or sudden swelling if renal failure develops. In malaria, fever spikes are common.
Key tests confirm haemolysis, rule out immune causes, and identify the underlying trigger. When resources are limited, a smear and basic biochemistry can still guide urgent therapy.

t.b: Negative in MAHA, positive in autoimmune haemolysis
Low in TTP, normal in HUS

sections.p: Rapidly rising creatinine, severe hypertension, seizures, or shock demand immediate transfer. Untreated MAHA can lead to multi‑organ failure and death.

Treat the underlying cause first: antimalarials for malaria, antibiotics for bacterial infections, or plasma exchange for TTP/HUS. Supportive care includes transfusion of washed red cells, platelet transfusion only if bleeding, and renal replacement if needed.

t.b: Removes autoantibodies and microthrombi in TTP/HUS

sections.p: Monitor haemoglobin, platelets, LDH, and renal function weekly. Prevent re‑infection with malaria prophylaxis, treat HIV, and counsel against nephrotoxic herbal remedies.
Immune haemolytic anaemia (positive Coombs), hereditary spherocytosis, and thalassaemia can mimic MAHA but lack schistocytes and thrombocytopenia.
Normal platelet count can occur early; haptoglobin may be low in chronic liver disease, masking haemolysis. Coombs can be falsely negative if low antibody levels.
